```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Use this guide when adapting an existing login, selecting between accounts,
or saving query results between user actions. For a first app, choose a
source in [Getting started](getting-started.html); each source guide
includes its own sign-in setup.

## Keep an existing login

The `*_client()` helpers provide optional sign-in configurations. If you
already use shinyOAuth, keep your provider, client, UI, and server module.
The token must be intended for the database or API you're calling.

In shinyOAuth, named **token targets** let one authorization obtain tokens
for different services. Microsoft's presets use names such as `"sql"`
and `"storage"`. If your existing SQL target is named `"reporting"`,
select it explicitly:

```{r custom-sql-target}
con <- oauth_db_azure_sql(
  auth$connection,
  server = "example.database.windows.net",
  database = "Reporting",
  target = "reporting"
)
```

For a client without named targets, use `target = NULL` with a suitable
default token. The [Fabric guide](fabric.html#connection-options-and-custom-sign-in)
shows its API client's service-to-target mapping.

## Request and check permissions

OAuth scopes describe the permissions your app requests from the provider.
Configure them on the shinyOAuth client or its token targets. The presets
supply defaults for the selected services; replace these when your
registration requires different settings.

A helper's `required_scopes` argument checks permissions before use. It
doesn't request consent or add database privileges. The shinyOAuth client
and target still enforce their configured requirements.

Microsoft's `/.default` requests the registration's configured permissions;
it isn't a granted permission name. Don't put it in `required_scopes`.
The [Snowflake guide](snowflake.html#external-oauth) explains its role scopes.

## Select among several accounts

Use shinyOAuth's connection manager when a visitor should retain several
authorizations. See
`vignette("multiple-authorizations", package = "shinyOAuth")` for manager setup.

Pass a function that selects the database authorization:

```{r selected-account}
con <- oauth_db_azure_sql(
  function() auth$connection(shiny::req(input$authorization_id)),
  server = "example.database.windows.net",
  database = "Reporting"
)
```

Populate the selector with `connection_id` values from `auth$connections()`.
These identify saved authorizations, rather than token targets such as
`"sql"`. Create separate helpers for different selected accounts if needed.

## Clear stored results

Outputs that call a connection helper or API client in their reactive
expression follow sign-in changes. Data your app has already fetched needs
separate care: if you save results in `reactiveVal()`, `eventReactive()`,
or another cache, clear or hide them when the selected authorization ends
or changes. A cache keyed only by SQL text can share protected data between
users.

The source checkout's `playground/example-query-button.R` shows a query
button that clears results on sign-out, account changes, and loss of required
permissions. `playground/example-two-authorizations.R` shows independent
SQL and Databricks authorizations.

## Refresh and longer work

shinyOAuth renews tokens. Call `con()` before each operation so the helper
can check the current authorization and replace a connection when needed.
The source guides describe how their clients use refreshed credentials.

`min_valid_for` asks for enough remaining token lifetime when obtaining a
credential; it doesn't guarantee validity for a whole query. If a refresh
is already running, accessors wait quietly and ordinary reactive consumers
can resume when it finishes. Event-bound code may need another click.

Previously returned handles and copied token strings follow their own
package's rules. Local sign-out doesn't necessarily invalidate those copies
or cancel work already submitted to a platform.

Keep live connections and session-bound token callbacks in their owning
Shiny session. For background work, use the database package's supported
approach and check the current authorization before displaying a result.
